title: Gathering Scientific Information
seo_title: Primary 3 Basic Science: Gathering Scientific Information Worksheets (NERDC)
standard_code: Primary 3 Basic Science: Science and Development
standard_text: Science and technology have given us useful inventions. Pupils gather scientific information by observing, measuring with standard units, recording data in tables and charts, and drawing conclusions from evidence. (summary of the Basic Science curriculum, Primary 3, theme: Science and Development)
meta_desc: Free Primary 3 Basic Science worksheets (NERDC curriculum, theme: Science and Development): inventions, measuring, recording data in tables and charts, and drawing conclusions. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Scientists gather information carefully and record it.
key_sub: Measure with standard units such as metres and grams.
body_html:
How to think about it

Inventions such as the light bulb, the telephone and vaccines came from people who asked questions and tested ideas. Nigerian scientists also do research, for example on better crops at the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA) in Ibadan.

To gather scientific information, we observe and measure using standard units (metres, grams, litres, degrees Celsius). We record data in tables, bar graphs and charts, look for patterns, and draw a conclusion that matches the evidence.

Example

Which unit measures the mass of a melon?

Heavy things

Answer: kilograms

Example

Why record data in a table?

Easy to compare

Answer: it makes the data easy to read and compare

Common mistakes

  • Using a non-standard unit such as a hand span when others must compare.
  • Drawing a conclusion that the data do not show.
  • Changing more than one thing in a fair test.

faq.a: A test where only one thing is changed and everything else is kept the same.
To check our results and make them more reliable.

items.q: In a fair test, how many things should you change?
items.e: Change one, keep the rest the same.

items.q: A table has the heading 'Time'. What is missing?
items.e: Always write units in table headings.

items.q: What is a prediction?
c: what you think will happen, based on what you already know
items.e: Make a prediction before the test.

items.q: What is the best way to present the number of each kind of minibeast found under a log?
items.e: Bar charts compare amounts; tables record results; labelled diagrams name parts; keys identify things.

items.q: Which is an observation, not a conclusion?
c: Ice always melts fastest in foil.
The ice in the foil cup melted after 20 minutes.
items.e: An observation is what you saw or measured.

items.q: Which of these questions CANNOT be answered by a scientific test?
c: Does the temperature of water change how fast sugar dissolves?
Does salt water freeze faster than tap water?
Which day of the week is the best?
Does the type of surface change how far a ball rolls?
items.e: Opinions cannot be measured with a fair test.

items.q: Which equipment measures time?
items.e: Seconds and minutes.

items.q: Which equipment measures how much liquid there is?
items.e: Millilitres (ml).

items.q: Why do scientists repeat a test several times?
c: to check the results are reliable
because the first result is always wrong
items.e: Repeated results that agree are more trustworthy.

items.q: Why do scientists write results in a table?
c: to keep them organised and easy to read
items.e: Record as you go.

items.q: Which of these questions can be answered by a fair test?
c: Do people like the smell of eucalyptus?
Does the amount of sunlight change how tall bean plants grow?
Is science more fun than art?
Which day of the week is the best?
items.e: A testable question changes one thing and measures another.

items.q: What is the best way to present the temperature readings of a cup every 5 minutes?
items.e: Bar charts compare amounts; tables record results; labelled diagrams name parts; keys identify things.

items.q: What is the best way to present which materials did and did not conduct electricity?
items.e: Bar charts compare amounts; tables record results; labelled diagrams name parts; keys identify things.

items.q: What is the best way to present how many seconds ice cubes took to melt in four different wrappings?
items.e: Bar charts compare amounts; tables record results; labelled diagrams name parts; keys identify things.

items.q: Which is the safest way to heat water in a classroom test?
c: with an adult, using a kettle and heat-proof gloves
in a microwave in a closed metal tin
on your own with a candle
holding a glass over a flame
items.e: Plan safety before you start.

items.q: What is a scientific question?
c: a question you can answer by observing or testing
items.e: For example: does salt make ice melt faster?

items.q: Which of these questions CANNOT be answered by a scientific test?
c: Does the height of a ramp change how far a toy car rolls?
Do people like the smell of eucalyptus?
Does the type of surface change how far a ball rolls?
Does the temperature of water change how fast sugar dissolves?
items.e: Opinions cannot be measured with a fair test.

items.q: What is the best way to present how to identify six garden birds?
items.e: Bar charts compare amounts; tables record results; labelled diagrams name parts; keys identify things.

items.q: Which equipment measures temperature?
items.e: Read in °C.

items.q: Which of these questions CANNOT be answered by a scientific test?
c: Does the amount of sunlight change how tall bean plants grow?
Does the temperature of water change how fast sugar dissolves?
Does salt water freeze faster than tap water?
Which colour is the nicest for a bedroom wall?
items.e: Opinions cannot be measured with a fair test.

items.q: Chioma records the temperature of water in the sun every 10 minutes: 20, 24, 27, 29 °C. What pattern does she see?
c: The water gets warmer over time.
items.e: Each reading is higher than the one before.

items.q: What is a conclusion?
c: a sentence that says what the results show
items.e: It answers the question.

items.q: Before a test, Nkechi says, 'I think the ice will melt fastest in the sun.' What is this?
items.e: A prediction is what you think will happen.

items.q: How long is the pencil?
items.e: Read the mark at the end of the pencil.

items.q: Why do we write results in a table?
c: so we do not need to measure
to keep them neat and easy to compare
items.e: Tables have headings with units.

items.q: How long is the pencil?
items.e: Read the mark at the end of the pencil.

items.q: Ada's table: Brand A 30 mL, Brand B 45 mL, Brand C 20 mL. Which soaks up the most?
items.e: 45 mL is the largest amount.
Read the mark at the end of the red liquid.

items.q: How long is the pencil?
items.e: Read the mark at the end of the pencil.
Read the mark at the end of the red liquid.

items.q: In Obinna's test, what should he measure?
c: how much water each towel soaks up
items.e: Measure the result.

items.q: What should you do if one result is very different from the others?
c: check it by doing the test again
items.e: Repeating checks for mistakes.

items.q: What is a fair test?
c: a test where you change only one thing and keep everything else the same
a test where you change everything
items.e: Then you know what caused the result.

items.q: Tobi tests which paper towel soaks up the most water. What should he change?
items.e: Change one thing.

items.q: How long is the pencil?
items.e: Read the mark at the end of the pencil.

items.q: Usman says, 'Brand B is the best paper towel for everything.' Why is this not a good conclusion?
c: He did not use a table.
He only tested how much water it soaks up.
Brand B soaked up the least.
items.e: A conclusion must match what was tested.

items.q: Which tool should you use to measure the length of a leaf?
items.e: Length is measured in millimetres or centimetres.
Read the mark at the end of the red liquid.

items.q: Nkechi's group and Dayo's group get different results for the same test. What should they do?
c: compare their methods and repeat the test
items.e: Comparing methods finds mistakes.
Read the mark at the end of the red liquid.

items.q: Which conclusion matches the data: 'the bigger the jar, the longer the candle burned'?

items.q: A group measured the time for sugar to dissolve in warm water three times: 87 s, 83 s, 91 s. What is the average?
items.e: Add the results and divide by 3: 261 ÷ 3 = 87.
